title: Bootstrap dfui: menu bar free-disk indicator
description:
Stand up the repo and ship the smallest useful version of dfui: a macOS menu bar item showing free space on the volume holding /, formatted as free-to-2-significant-digits over total-to-1-significant-digit in decimal TB (e.g. 0.35/2TB).

Motivation: parallel LLM agent sessions writing Rust accumulate cargo target/ directories worth hundreds of GB; free disk needs to be glanceable without running df.

Plan: claude-notes/plans/2026-08-14-bootstrap.md
acceptance_criteria:
- Menu bar item renders e.g. 0.35/2TB and refreshes periodically
- No Dock icon (LSUIElement)
- Builds and runs with Command Line Tools only, no Xcode
- ./scripts/build-app.sh produces a launchable dist/dfui.app
- swift run selftest passes
close_reason: Scaffolding and v0 indicator landed in commit 07df153; app builds, runs, and shows 0.97/2TB

title: Make the low-space threshold configurable
description:
lowSpaceFraction is hardcoded at 0.05 (~100 GB on a 2 TB disk), which is what the user asked for initially. Worth making configurable eventually.

Design notes when picking this up:
- A fraction is the wrong knob on a small disk: 5% of 500 GB is 25 GB, which is already inside the zone where macOS misbehaves. Consider max(fraction * total, absolute floor) with a floor around 25-50 GB.
- Two levels (warn/critical) may be more useful than one, e.g. yellow at 5% and red at 1%.
- Storage: UserDefaults is the low-ceremony option; a menu submenu with a few preset thresholds avoids building a settings window.

title: Drill-down: what is eating the disk
description:
The indicator answers 'am I low?' but not 'what do I delete?'. The answer is almost always cargo target/ directories.

Sketch: a menu listing the largest target/ dirs under the user's repo roots with sizes, and a way to cargo clean or rm them from the menu. Needs care around doing destructive things from a menu bar item — at minimum a confirmation, and never a bare rm -rf on a path computed without validation.
close_reason: Implemented in e6a3737; scan + HTML report, verified end to end via --scan

c-2lvj3mui.author: Carlos Scheidegger
c-2lvj3mui.text:
Landed in e6a3737. Scan menu item + --scan CLI; HTML report to temp dir, opened in browser; no deletion, only cargo clean commands to review.

Key finding: of 33 dirs named 'target', only 25 were cargo build output. Five of the rest were ~/.cargo/registry/src/.../cc-*/src/target — source dirs inside cached crates. Naive name matching would have suggested deleting them. isCargoTarget checks CACHEDIR.TAG and sibling Cargo.toml (both agreed on all 33); rejects are listed in the report, not dropped silently.

Perf, measured on a 745 GB home dir: one filtered 'du -k -x' pass = 47s, versus 29s (find + per-target du) + 46s (separate depth-2 du) for the two-pass approach. Spotlight is much faster (0.19s) but incomplete — 10 of 13 targets under ~/repos — so unused.

First real run: 25 targets, 492 GB reclaimable.

Not verified: the menu click path itself (menu items aren't scriptable here). It shares writeReport/finishScan with the tested --scan path.

title: Decide: statfs vs volumeAvailableCapacityForImportantUsage
description:
dfui currently reads free space via statfs(2)'s f_bavail, matching df -h /, because that is the user's reference point.

macOS's recommended API is URLResourceValues.volumeAvailableCapacityForImportantUsageKey, which is what Finder and About This Mac report. It counts purgeable space (Time Machine local snapshots, caches macOS will evict under pressure) as available, so it reads meaningfully higher than df.

Which number is more useful for the actual purpose here — noticing when cargo target/ dirs have eaten the disk? Purgeable space is real headroom the OS will reclaim, so the Finder number may be less alarmist but more honest. Worth deciding deliberately rather than by default.

Consider also showing both, or making it a preference.
close_reason: Decided: keep statfs; gap is 0.1 GB on this machine and the conservative number is correct for an alarm (a90ede0)

c-geyk1bqo.author: Carlos Scheidegger
c-geyk1bqo.text: Settled: keeping statfs. Measured on the machine — statfs f_bavail 969.6 GB vs volumeAvailableCapacityForImportantUsage 969.7 GB, a 0.1 GB gap, because Time Machine has no destination configured so nothing is purgeable. The two differ only by purgeable space; statfs is the conservative reading (writable now, no OS reclamation assumed), which is the right basis for an alarm, and it keeps 'df -h /' a valid cross-check. Revisit only if Time Machine is enabled. Side note: volumeAvailableCapacityForOpportunisticUsage reads ~12 GB below plain available — macOS's own headroom estimate.

title: Run dfui at login
description:
The app has to be launched manually today. For an always-visible indicator it should start at login.

Options: SMAppService.mainApp.register() (modern, needs the bundle in a stable location), or a LaunchAgent plist in ~/Library/LaunchAgents. Also decide where the built .app should live — dist/ inside the repo is fine for development but a login item pointing into a working tree is fragile; consider installing to /Applications or ~/Applications.
close_reason: Implemented and verified in b2d9f0e; install to ~/Applications plus Open at Login toggle

c-ss7nyyw8.author: Carlos Scheidegger
c-ss7nyyw8.text: Landed in b2d9f0e. SMAppService.mainApp works with an ad-hoc signature from ~/Applications — no Developer ID, no /Applications, and status lands in .enabled with no approval step. Registration survives replacing the bundle, so install.sh does not re-register. Not visible in launchctl list (BTM is not a user launchd domain); use 'dfui --login-item status'. Untested: actual launch on boot, which needs a reboot.

title: Color/threshold warning when free space gets low
description: Once the indicator exists, the next step in usefulness is making it demand attention only when it should: tint the text (or swap in an icon) below a configurable threshold, so a glance is enough and the number itself can be ignored most of the time.
close_reason: Implemented in a90ede0: red + bold + GB unit switch below 5%, with --simulate-free-gb for verification

title: Guard against two dfui instances running at once
description:
Nothing stops the dist/ copy and the ~/Applications copy from running simultaneously, which puts two identical indicators in the menu bar. Easy to hit during development: build, run from dist/, then install and launch, and now there are two.

Fix: on launch, check NSRunningApplication for another instance with the same bundle identifier and either exit or terminate the older one. Note the check must tolerate the bare 'swift run dfui' case, which has no bundle identifier.
close_reason: Fixed in 87b769f; newest-wins termination on launch, verified in both directions

c-8u5kpdhm.author: Carlos Scheidegger
c-8u5kpdhm.text:
Landed in 87b769f. Verified both directions (dist -> ~/Applications and reverse) leave exactly one instance, and that an unbundled 'swift run dfui' is left alone.

Two findings worth keeping: NSRunningApplication.current.launchDate is nil for a directly exec'd process, so the PID tiebreak is the ordinary path rather than a fallback; and NSWorkspace reports 16 node processes with a nil bundle identifier, so matching nil-against-nil would have terminated all of them — hence the unbundled exemption.

title: Migrate selftest to swift-testing once Xcode is installed
description:
Tests currently live in Sources/selftest as a plain executable with a hand-rolled assertion harness, because neither swift-testing nor XCTest ships with the Command Line Tools — a .testTarget cannot build without a full Xcode install.

If Xcode is ever installed on this machine, replace Sources/selftest with a proper .testTarget using swift-testing and restore 'swift test'. Until then this is blocked on a decision the user may never want to make (Xcode is a large install for a project this size).
